title: Classification
subtitle: Topic: Classification · Subject: Supervised Machine Learning. Three beginner, two medium and two advanced questions with original visual explanations, balanced alternatives, and a tested scikit-learn example.
hero:
CLASSIFICATION · VISUAL STUDY

Learn categories from examples, then choose a label

Classification is supervised prediction of discrete labels. A trained model uses input features to estimate scores or probabilities, makes a decision, and needs careful evaluation when class frequencies or mistake costs differ.

questions.stem: What is Classification in supervised machine learning, and how do input features and known target labels help a model categorize new examples?
options: Classification estimates a continuously varying quantity such as price or rainfall and rounds it to a category only at reporting time. Training labels are unnecessary because numerical predictions provide their own supervision.

Classification groups examples without known outcomes, then asks an optimizer to invent class labels using distances between features. It cannot be trained with actual categories because that would change the task into regression.

Classification learns a relationship between input features and discrete target categories using labeled examples. It can assign a new email a class such as spam or not spam, sometimes using predicted class probabilities.

Classification stores the label for each training example and returns the closest stored label without learning any reusable prediction rule. Its predictions therefore require every new input to appear exactly in the training data.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Classification is supervised learning that predicts a discrete category. Each training example has features describing the case and a target label giving its known category. A model learns patterns linking those features to labels, then uses them on new inputs. For example, a spam filter can learn from emails already labeled spam or legitimate and estimate a class for a new message. A classifier may output class probabilities as well as a final label. Predicting the number of minutes an email takes to deliver would instead be regression.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 01 · CLASSIFICATION

A supervised classifier learns from inputs paired with known categories. For a new email it receives features, predicts a spam probability and then a class; the label is not supplied as a feature.

questions.stem: How do binary, multiclass, and multi-label Classification differ in the number of classes and whether multiple labels may be true for one example?
options: Binary classification chooses one of two labels; multiclass chooses one among three or more mutually exclusive labels; multi-label classification can assign several independent labels to the same example, such as dog and tree.

Binary classification always predicts two independent labels simultaneously, while multiclass prediction permits every category to be true. Multi-label classification instead requires a single selected category from at least three possible outputs.

Binary, multiclass and multi-label classification all require exactly one true class per example. They differ only in the number of training samples available and therefore use interchangeable target encodings in every task.

Binary classification requires a single numeric measurement, multiclass classification predicts a real number for each category, and multi-label classification transforms those numbers into one continuous prediction rather than a set of categories.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Binary classification means a single choice between two categories, such as approved or rejected. Multiclass classification still assigns one exclusive category but offers at least three, such as cat, dog or bird. Multi-label classification is different: multiple independent tags can all be correct. A photograph could contain both a dog and a tree, so its label vector might be [1,0,1]. Understanding this distinction helps select the right output activation, target representation and loss function instead of using one method for every category task.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 02 · CLASSIFICATION

Binary classification predicts one of two labels. Multiclass predicts one among three or more exclusive labels. Multi-label classification makes independent label decisions, allowing more than one positive.

questions.stem: How do class scores, softmax probabilities, argmax, and decision thresholds relate when a Classification model makes a prediction?
options: Raw model scores are always valid probabilities, even if they are negative or exceed one. Softmax only changes their display format, and argmax chooses the class closest to the average score.
Softmax converts every class score independently using a sigmoid, so probabilities may exceed a total of one. Argmax chooses every class above a threshold and guarantees the results are calibrated.
Decision thresholds change the fitted model weights every time a new case is evaluated. Argmax compares the input features directly, without using scores or probabilities from the trained classifier.

Raw scores can be normalized by softmax for exclusive multiclass probabilities, with argmax selecting the largest score. A binary classifier may instead compare positive-class probability with a chosen threshold to decide its label.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A classifier can produce raw numerical scores for its categories. For a mutually exclusive multiclass task, softmax turns those scores into probabilities summing to one, and argmax selects the most likely class. In a binary task, a sigmoid probability can be compared with a decision threshold such as 0.50. Changing the threshold changes decisions without necessarily retraining the model. A high probability score does not automatically mean it is well calibrated: calibration must be assessed against observed outcomes on held-out data.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 03 · CLASSIFICATION

Softmax can normalize multiclass logits into a distribution and argmax chooses the largest score. Binary classifiers can compare a positive-class probability against a decision threshold such as 0.50.

questions.tag: Medium · Interpreting a multiclass confusion matrix
questions.stem: How can a confusion matrix reveal Classification errors across three classes, and what accuracy follows from diagonal counts 28, 16 and 8 among 60 test examples?
options: Each diagonal cell records a class's false positives, while off-diagonal cells are correct predictions. The accuracy is therefore the total off-diagonal count, 8 divided by 60, or about 13.3%.

With true labels on rows and predicted labels on columns, diagonal cells count correct predictions. The diagonal sums to 52 of 60, giving about 86.7% accuracy; off-diagonal cells expose class confusions.

Accuracy equals the largest diagonal entry divided by all test cases, so this matrix gives 28/60 or about 46.7%. Errors cannot be identified from a three-class confusion matrix without probability scores.
Every row of a confusion matrix lists one model's predictions rather than an actual class. Accuracy is the average of diagonal counts, giving (28+16+8)/3, or about 17.3%.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A confusion matrix compares actual classes with predicted classes. Here rows are actual labels and columns are predictions. Entries on the diagonal are correct; the others show which labels the model confuses. The diagonal has 28+16+8=52 correct predictions out of 60, so accuracy is approximately 86.7%. In the third row, only 8 of 12 actual class-2 examples were recognized, giving recall 66.7%. This is why looking at one overall accuracy figure can hide weaker performance for a particular category.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 04 · CLASSIFICATION

Rows are actual labels, columns are predictions. The diagonal 28+16+8 gives 52 correct of 60, so accuracy is 86.7%; off-diagonal entries identify which categories are confused.

questions.stem: How should a Classification model be trained and evaluated with scikit-learn so preprocessing stays leakage-free and test metrics reflect unseen examples?
options: Fit the StandardScaler using all labeled examples before a train/test split, then train the classifier only on training labels. Tuning on the test confusion matrix is acceptable because a Pipeline prevents leakage automatically.

Split the dataset, fit an independent scaler on each test subset, and train LogisticRegression using only the normalized testing features. Test accuracy remains unbiased as long as labels are used only for reporting.

Split labeled examples, fit StandardScaler and LogisticRegression together inside a training pipeline, and predict held-out cases without refitting. Report confusion matrix, accuracy and macro F1 on that separate test set.

Train LogisticRegression using all data, then randomly assign some examples to a test subset afterward. The model's test metric is reliable because class probabilities remain normalized even after training sees those examples.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The safe workflow is to split data before fitting preprocessing or a classifier. In scikit-learn, a Pipeline fits StandardScaler on the training features and trains LogisticRegression using those transformed examples. It then transforms held-out cases with the same learned scaling. In the tested 240-example synthetic dataset, 180 examples train the model and 60 form the holdout. The results are accuracy 0.867 and macro F1 0.839. The confusion matrix reveals class-specific mistakes, and the test set is never used for fitting.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 05 · CLASSIFICATION
scikit-learn · Three-class classification pipeline 15 lines
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=240, n_features=6,
    n_informative=4, n_redundant=0, n_classes=3,
    n_clusters_per_class=1, weights=[.5,.3,.2],
    class_sep=.9, flip_y=.05, random_state=12)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, stratify=y, random_state=11)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=500))
pred = model.fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte)
print(confusion_matrix(yte, pred).tolist())
print(round(accuracy_score(yte, pred),3), round(f1_score(yte, pred, average="macro"),3))

The scikit-learn example fits scaling and logistic regression on 180 training examples. The 60 held-out examples yield accuracy 0.867 and macro F1 0.839, with a full three-class confusion matrix.

questions.stem: Why can Classification accuracy be deceptive when one class is rare, and which evaluation measures help expose failure to detect important minority cases?
options: If 95 of 100 examples are negative, predicting every case negative produces 95% accuracy but zero positive recall. Per-class recall, precision, balanced accuracy, and F1 help expose performance hidden by class imbalance.

Accuracy automatically adjusts for class imbalance because it gives minority examples larger statistical weight. A classifier that always predicts negative would score only 50% accuracy when positives are rare.
Rare-class errors cannot be measured with precision or recall because those metrics need equal class sizes. Overall accuracy is sufficient as long as a model uses a stratified train/test split.

Predicting all examples as the majority class proves the model has excellent calibration when its accuracy is high. Adjusting thresholds or inspecting error costs is unnecessary because accuracy already accounts for them.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Accuracy measures the proportion of all correct predictions, so a common class can dominate it. If 95 examples are negative and 5 are positive, always predicting negative gets 95% accuracy while missing every positive. Positive recall is 0%, and balanced accuracy is only 50% because it averages recall across the two classes. For an equipment-failure warning system, those missed faults may be costly. Examine precision, recall, F1, balanced accuracy, and error costs rather than trusting one impressive overall score.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 06 · CLASSIFICATION

If 95 of 100 examples are negative, a model predicting every case negative achieves 95% accuracy but finds none of five positives. Positive recall is 0% and balanced accuracy is 50%.

questions.tag: Advanced · Leakage, calibration and real-world reliability
questions.stem: How should a Classification system handle training, validation, testing, probability calibration, related records and deployment monitoring to obtain trustworthy performance?
options: Fit feature transformations on the complete dataset before splitting to preserve consistency, then choose model settings using test accuracy. Once softmax probabilities sum to one, they are calibrated and need no later monitoring.

Train the model on all available examples, evaluate on a random subset already included in fitting, and choose thresholds from those results. Group leakage is harmless when the classifier has multiple output categories.

Use test examples to choose decision thresholds and calibration methods, then report those same examples as an unbiased evaluation. Once a model is deployed, class proportions can change without affecting performance estimates.

Fit transformations and model parameters on training data, tune choices and calibration on validation data, and reserve an untouched test set for final evaluation. Use time or group splits when appropriate and monitor drift after deployment.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Reliable classification depends on the entire evaluation process. Fit preprocessing and model parameters using training data. Use validation data for model selection, decision thresholds and probability calibration checks. Keep the test set untouched until the final estimate. When examples from one customer or future time period are related, choose group-aware or chronological splits to prevent leakage. After deployment, monitor class frequency, calibration, false alarms and missed detections. Even a predicted probability of 0.90 needs empirical validation before treating it as trustworthy.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 07 · CLASSIFICATION

Split appropriately before fitting transformations. Use validation data to tune models and thresholds and assess probability calibration. Keep test data untouched until final evaluation, then monitor drift and error costs in deployment.
